reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Manuscript by Ding et al.
Title: Paleomagnetic evidence for Neoarchean plate mobilism
This manuscript presents a new 2.48 Ga paleomagnetic pole from the Elbow Creek mafic dykes of the
Wyoming carton. The paleomagnetic data presented here is of high-quality (key pole), with a positive
field stability test (positive baked contact test). The new 2.48 Ga pole is used here to explore the relative
horizontal plate motions between crustal blocks (Wyoming and Superior cratons) and the data is used to
study the operation of plate tectonics. (i.e., plate mobilism). Based on differing paleomagnetic apparent
polar wander paths of Wyoming and Superior in during 2.7-2.5 Ga authors make a well justified
suggestion that the plate tectonics was in operation prior to 2.5 Ga.
Plate tectonics have had major impact on Earth’s geologic, climatic and biologic record, but onset time
of plate tectonics is debated. Time estimates range from the Hadean to the Neoproterozoic depending
on the used proxy (e.g., geology, geochemistry, paleomagnetism, geodynamic models). The results from
this study will interest many people in several geoscience disciplines as the onset of plate tectonics is
one of the major questions in the Earth sciences. As geological record of the operation of plate tectonic
may have been lost, the paleomagnetic method remains one of the most robust methods to explore the
relative horizontal motion of tectonic plates (i.e. plate tectonics) at Archean.
The manuscript is well written and it is an excellent and clear compilation of data. By combining
paleomagnetic data with proxies for lithospheric rigidity and petrological and metamorphic evidence for
subduction the manuscript presents a very nice study of the onset of plate tectonics. Illustration of the
manuscript is of very high quality, especially Figure 3, which combines proxies for plate tectonics.
The chosen selection between main body text and supplementary information is adequate.
I have one major concern and few minor comments on the manuscript.
Baked contact test.
Baked contact tests are the key for this study in providing proofs of the primary magnetization. Authors
claim that there are positive baked contact tests for the dykes J20S24 (cutting anorthosite, ca. 2710 Ma
Stillwater Complex) and J20S28 (cutting granite, ca 2800 Ma Mouat quartz monzonite in Fig. 1).
Dyke J20S24. Authors write that the samples from the site J21S12 (baked anorthosite) yielded an HTC
that is directed SE and down with moderate inclination, broadly similar to that of the dyke. However,
the mean directions from the dyke and from the baked host rock seem to be 40 apart (Fig. S6) and their
alpha95 confidence cones are not overlapping. Therefore, the directions are not the same and this does
not support a positive baked contact test.
Dyke J20S28. This dyke site shows more convincing positive baked contact test than the dyke J20S24.
However, the unbaked direction is obtained only from three samples. Please discuss this.
How reliable are the unbaked directions from these sites? There are only three unbaked samples for the
dyke J20S28, more for the dyke J20S24. Directions obtained from unbaked samples for these dykes are
very different. Please address this.
Minor comments:
Both AF and TH methods were used for cleaning the magnetization and authors choose to use only TH
results because there is difference between these. The manuscript is lacking a discussing of possible
reasons for this, and it should be added. Moreover, if only TH method is used to define the pole, the
criteria #2 of Meert et al (2021) is not fulfilled and the pole scores 0 from this criterion  fulfils 5 of the 7
seven criteria. Not 6 as indicated in the manuscript.
Line 226 (supplementary). Dyke JLQ15? Should it be the dyke J20S24?
Lines 231-232. There is some words missing from the sentence starting: ”The HTCs of the baked samples
from sites J20S12, J20S15…”
Lines 243-259: Confusion with component B and component C. Text reads as: “…with dike J20S14,
the results suggest that its HTC (component B) should be primary…” “…high-temperature component C from
dike J20S14 should be primary…”
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Overview:
The study presented by Ding et al., on ‘Paleomagnetic evidence for Neoarchean plate mobilism’
presents new paleomagnetic data from a suite of dykes that intrude the Stillwater Complex on the
Wyoming craton. The authors identify 4 distinct high-temperature components in the dyke
demagnetization at different sites, which they refer to as Component A, Component B, Component
C and Component D. They use a baked contact test and fold test to argue that Component A is
primary and has not experienced subsequent remagnetization after emplacement ca. 2480 Ma.
Components B, C and D are attributed to various events by comparing the recovered directions with
those of other well-dated events: Component B is also thought to be a similar age to the Stillwater
complex, Component C is associated with the 2210 Ma Claye Butte dykes and Component D is
associated with the ca. 780 Ma Gunbarrel dykes.
The authors argue that their new paleopole at 2.48 Ga provides evidence for the joining together of the
Wyoming and Superior cratons, requiring at least 30° of lateral motion since 2.71 Ga. While the
approach presented here is a good one for addressing relative plate motions in the Archean, many lines
of argument are hard to follow, figures are mis-cited, and I have some significant concerns about the
interpretation of paleomagnetic results. I outline major comments below, which should be addressed
before this can be considered for publication, followed by minor line-by-line comments. If the authors
can address these comments then I believe this manuscript may still be suitable for publication at
Nature Communications, since evidence for early plate tectonics is sufficiently controversial and of wide
interest to the scientific community.
Major Comments:
The timing and evidence for previous locations of the Wyoming and Superior cratons needs to be
explained in substantially more detail. For example, it is really not clear to me when reading the
manuscript where the constraint on the location of the two cratons comes from for 2.71 Ga? The data
shown in Figure 3B and 3C in the main text needs to be explained in more detail to explain which
constraints are from this study versus those from existing literature. It is also not clear how a palepole
constraint for 2.48 Ga makes the argument for the lateral movement of these cratons relative to one
another stronger than it was from existing paleopoles. Please clarify.
The new paleomagnetic data presented here is generally nice – I agree with the interpretation of
stable magnetic carriers, and recovery of a unidirectional component ‘Component A’. However, there are many
sweeping statements that are not supported by the data as it stands. In particular, these include
comparing directions e.g., the 2.48 Ga direction to that recovered from the 2.71 Ga Stillwater complex.
Both directions need to be stated, and shown to be different with statistical significance (e.g., by
calculating Watson’s VW statistic). Similarly, it is stated that the baked contact tests pass, even though
they appear ambiguous and no statistical tests are carried out. In almost all cases, the baked directions
do not agree with the dyke direction – an explanation needs to be given for this. Similarly, the expected
width of the baked regions, and the width of the dykes are not stated. While the baked contact tests do
not clearly ‘pass’, neither do they clearly fail. This somewhat weakens the results presented here, but
doesn’t nullify them. I recommend the authors re-phrase their interpretation of the results to make it
clear they’re not without uncertainty.
The origin of Components B is difficult to follow. This direction does not appear to be unidirectional,
and I am also unclear on the discussion of which age this component corresponds to. Is it thought to
be older than Component A? In addition, can you include fold tests for components B, C and D in order to
comment on their timing of remanence acquisition relative to tilting? This will strengthen your
arguments regarding their interpreted ages.
The paleopole presented here was calculated from 100% untilted directions, even though the maximum
degree of clustering was found at 20% untilting. I disagree with the authors’ interpretation that this is
evidence for dyke emplacement after tilting – it looks much more like dyke emplacement syn-tilting to
me. I would like to see a paleopole reconstruction for this maximum clustering at 20% untilting. How
much does this change things?
The authors are a little vague on their definition of tectonics in terms of a large degree of lateral
motion. It would be nice to see upper/lower limits on plate motion calculated from the extent of
lateral motion inferred here, and a discussion of how that fits in with present day tectonic motions.
I think this would add real significance to the results presented here.
Main Text Comments:
Line 61-62 – can you clarify how this is a comparison between two separate blocks? Since you are
only providing new measurements here for one locality, it needs to be made clearer how this will be
compared to go above and beyond the studies of Brenner et al.,
Line 95-96 – which lithology was sampled in the Stillwater Complex? By ‘host rocks’ do you mean the
country rock that the dykes are intruded into? The phrasing could be clearer here.
Lines 120-121when you say Component A is ‘clearly distinct’ from that of the Stillwater Complex,
please state both dec, inc and alpha95s of recovered directions, I would recommend calculating
Watson’s Vw statistic to demonstrate that they are distinct with statistical significance. I’m assuming
the fact that Component A is distinct is highlighting that it is younger than the magnetization in the
host rocks? If so please clarify this in the main text.
Line 140 – Figure S15 referenced before S13 and S14, I am also not sure you mean S15 here, since it
provides no evidence for LIPs
Line 151-152 – given the timeframe and 30 degrees of separation, can you comment on the minimum
rate of plate motion required and how this compares to modern tectonics?
Line 166 – I think you mean to refer to Figure S14 here, not S13.
Line 164-168 and Figure S14 – I find this quite difficult to follow. I can see that the reconstructions
based on this method are non-unique, and this is nicely illustrated. However, even within the
ambiguity, these studies still appear to conclusively demonstrate relative motion between plates (i.e., there does not
seem to be any possible solution between 2775 Ma and 2440 Ma that does not involve differential
motion between the plates?). Also, why are ages out of order in Figure S14? This makes it very difficult
to follow!
Line 178-179 – how large is ‘large lateral mobility’? Is there a minimum rate of lateral motion that is
required to meet the definition of tectonics? How do your constraints on plate motion compare to this?
Line 203 – I don’t think you mean A2.3 here, since that’s the section on baked contact tests.
Supplementary Material Comments:
Figures S2D – for IRM acquisition, please plot dIRM/dB vs field. I would recommend using MAX UnMix to
identify the different coercivity populations in your samples (DOI: 10.1016/j.cageo.2016.07.009)
Please add more details in the figure caption for Figure S4 – there’s a lot going on here, and it’s difficult
to interpret the different components at the moment. Also please clarify what kind of projection is used,
and whether negative inclinations are projected in the top or bottom hemisphere.
Section A2.2.1 states that 12 dykes had a stable, SE trending HTC. However, only 6 of these are
shown in Figure S3. Please clarify. It would help significantly to show the identified components as
arrows on the zijdervelds, with zoom-ins of HTCs, and please plot all diagrams with same axes so they can be readily
compared.
Section A2.3 - why is the baked direction different to the dyke direction for dyke J20S24? Can you show
the LTC, MTC and HTC directions for the baked units as a function of distance from the dyke? How wide
do you expect the baked region to be – what is the width of the dyke, and what assumptions do you
make about heating of surrounding country rock? And why no samples between 1 and 100m?? Also
please calculate Watson’s Vw statistic for each site to show whether the dyke and baked direction are
the same and the unbaked direction distinct, and with what statistical significance.
Section A2.4 - when the tilt correction is applied, you find maximum clustering of directions 19.4%
and claim this suggests that the dykes post-date folding. This doesn’t make sense to me, surely this
implies that the dykes were emplaced in the early stages of tilting/folding, since after applying a
100% tilt correction your directions are significantly more dispersed than when they are not tilt
corrected at all? How does it impact your interpretation if the dykes are emplaced syn-tilting? How
does the pole calculated from the direction recovered from 20% untilting compare to that presented?
Does it change the implications of your results?
Section A2.5 – presumably taking into account the best clustered direction above will also strengthen
the results presented here?

depending on the used proxy (e.g., geology, geochemistry, paleomagnetism, geodynamic models).

operation of plate tectonic may have been lost, the paleomagnetic method remains one of the most
robust methods to explore the relative horizontal motion of tectonic plates (i.e. plate tectonics) at

Title: Paleomagnetic evidence for Neoarchean plate mobilism
This manuscript presents a new 2.48 Ga paleomagnetic pole from the Elbow Creek mafic dykes of the
Wyoming carton. The paleomagnetic data presented here is of high-quality (key pole), with a positive
field stability test (positive baked contact test). The new 2.48 Ga pole is used here to explore the relative
horizontal plate motions between crustal blocks (Wyoming and Superior cratons) and the data is used to
study the operation of plate tectonics. (i.e., plate mobilism). Based on differing paleomagnetic apparent
polar wander paths of Wyoming and Superior in during 2.7-2.5 Ga authors make a well justified
suggestion that the plate tectonics was in operation prior to 2.5 Ga.
Plate tectonics have had major impact on Earth’s geologic, climatic and biologic record, but onset time
of plate tectonics is debated. Time estimates range from the Hadean to the Neoproterozoic depending
on the used proxy (e.g., geology, geochemistry, paleomagnetism, geodynamic models). The results from
this study will interest many people in several geoscience disciplines as the onset of plate tectonics is
one of the major questions in the Earth sciences. As geological record of the operation of plate tectonic
may have been lost, the paleomagnetic method remains one of the most robust methods to explore the
relative horizontal motion of tectonic plates (i.e. plate tectonics) at Archean.
The manuscript is well written and it is an excellent and clear compilation of data. By combining
paleomagnetic data with proxies for lithospheric rigidity and petrological and metamorphic evidence for

manuscript is of very high quality, especially Figure 3, which combines proxies for plate tectonics.
The chosen selection between main body text and supplementary information is adequate.

### Reviewer 2

Overview:
The study presented by Ding et al., on ‘Paleomagnetic evidence for Neoarchean plate mobilism’
presents new paleomagnetic data from a suite of dykes that intrude the Stillwater Complex on the
Wyoming craton. The authors identify 4 distinct high-temperature components in the dyke
demagnetization at different sites, which they refer to as Component A, Component B, Component
C and Component D. They use a baked contact test and fold test to argue that Component A is
primary and has not experienced subsequent remagnetization after emplacement ca. 2480 Ma.
Components B, C and D are attributed to various events by comparing the recovered directions with
those of other well-dated events: Component B is also thought to be a similar age to the Stillwater
complex, Component C is associated with the 2210 Ma Claye Butte dykes and Component D is
associated with the ca. 780 Ma Gunbarrel dykes.
The authors argue that their new paleopole at 2.48 Ga provides evidence for the joining together of the
Wyoming and Superior cratons, requiring at least 30° of lateral motion since 2.71 Ga. While the
approach presented here is a good one for addressing relative plate motions in the Archean, many lines
of argument are hard to follow, figures are mis-cited, and I have some significant concerns about the
interpretation of paleomagnetic results. I outline major comments below, which should be addressed
before this can be considered for publication, followed by minor line-by-line comments. If the authors
can address these comments then I believe this manuscript may still be suitable for publication at
Nature Communications, since evidence for early plate tectonics is sufficiently controversial and of wide
interest to the scientific community.
Major Comments:
The timing and evidence for previous locations of the Wyoming and Superior cratons needs to be
explained in substantially more detail. For example, it is really not clear to me when reading the
manuscript where the constraint on the location of the two cratons comes from for 2.71 Ga? The data
shown in Figure 3B and 3C in the main text needs to be explained in more detail to explain which
constraints are from this study versus those from existing literature. It is also not clear how a palepole
constraint for 2.48 Ga makes the argument for the lateral movement of these cratons relative to one
another stronger than it was from existing paleopoles. Please clarify.
The new paleomagnetic data presented here is generally nice – I agree with the interpretation of
stable magnetic carriers, and recovery of a unidirectional component ‘Component A’. However, there are many
sweeping statements that are not supported by the data as it stands. In particular, these include
comparing directions e.g., the 2.48 Ga direction to that recovered from the 2.71 Ga Stillwater complex.
Both directions need to be stated, and shown to be different with statistical significance (e.g., by
calculating Watson’s VW statistic). Similarly, it is stated that the baked contact tests pass, even though
they appear ambiguous and no statistical tests are carried out. In almost all cases, the baked directions
do not agree with the dyke direction – an explanation needs to be given for this. Similarly, the expected
width of the baked regions, and the width of the dykes are not stated. While the baked contact tests do
not clearly ‘pass’, neither do they clearly fail. This somewhat weakens the results presented here, but
doesn’t nullify them. I recommend the authors re-phrase their interpretation of the results to make it
clear they’re not without uncertainty.
The origin of Components B is difficult to follow. This direction does not appear to be unidirectional,
and I am also unclear on the discussion of which age this component corresponds to. Is it thought to
be older than Component A? In addition, can you include fold tests for components B, C and D in order to
comment on their timing of remanence acquisition relative to tilting? This will strengthen your
arguments regarding their interpreted ages.
The paleopole presented here was calculated from 100% untilted directions, even though the maximum
degree of clustering was found at 20% untilting. I disagree with the authors’ interpretation that this is
evidence for dyke emplacement after tilting – it looks much more like dyke emplacement syn-tilting to

much does this change things?
The authors are a little vague on their definition of tectonics in terms of a large degree of lateral
motion. It would be nice to see upper/lower limits on plate motion calculated from the extent of
lateral motion inferred here, and a discussion of how that fits in with present day tectonic motions.
I think this would add real significance to the results presented here.
